Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantaviruses: Current insights, lessons from the MV Hondius outbreak, and an urgent call to action.
papers.abstract: In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infrastructure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical management, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases.

papers.full_text: Figures Abstract In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infrastructure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical management, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases. Citation: Chakravarty N, Vaithi V, Jeyachandran AV, Arunachalam R, Zaiss A, Bonazzi A, et al. (2026) Hantaviruses: Current insights, lessons from the MV Hondius outbreak, and an urgent call to action. PLoS Pathog 22(11): e1014756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 Editor: Wendy Maury, University of Iowa, UNITED STATES OF AMERICA Published: November 13, 2026 This is an open access article, free of all copyright, and may be freely reproduced, distributed, transmitted, modified, built upon, or otherwise used by anyone for any lawful purpose. The work is made available under the Creative Commons CC0 public domain dedication. Funding: This study was partially funded by NIH grants R01EY032149 and R01EY036572 to VA. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript. Competing interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist. A primer on the MV Hondius outbreak Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus capable of human-to-human transmission, underscoring its potential for outbreaks that extend beyond the traditional rodent-to-human route. This significance became particularly clear in May 2026, when the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of several cases of severe respiratory illness aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship carrying 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries, as it transited the South Atlantic from Argentina. Only a few days later, at least 13 cases, including three deaths, were identified and/or laboratory-confirmed, including secondary cases among contacts of the index patient [1], as well as plane passengers in close proximity to confirmed cases on a flight to South Africa [2] and a repatriation flight from Tenerife [1–6]. Contact tracing and quarantine measures were coordinated through the WHO National IHR (International Health Regulations) Focal Points and implemented across several countries, including the United Kingdom, South Africa, and the United States [2,3,7–10]. However, this outbreak is not the only recent notable case of hantaviral spread. In 2025, Betsy Arakawa, the wife of renowned actor Gene Hackman, passed away due to hantavirus infection in New Mexico, as did three people in Mammoth Lakes, California [11,12]. Hantavirus outbreaks highlight the challenge posed to public health agencies by neglected zoonotic pathogens—especially those that are ecologically complex, geographically distributed, understudied, and underfunded, yet capable of causing lethal outbreaks with little to no warning, thereby creating major public health concerns. As such, we aim to synthesize a brief primer on our current knowledge of hantaviruses and to propose areas for further research and development of emergency preparedness and capacity building within existing public health infrastructure. What we know Epidemiologic history and global burden of Hantaviruses Old World (e.g., Hantaan [HTNV], Puumala [PUUV], Dobrava, and Seoul [SEOV] virus) and New World (e.g., Sin Nombre virus [SNV], ANDV) hantaviruses are primarily carried and spread asymptomatically in rodent reservoirs. The history of hantaviruses can be traced back to the Korean War in the 1950s, when over 3,000 troops stationed along the Hantaan River fell ill with a previously unknown virus, now known as HTNV [13] (Fig 1). The first recorded outbreak of hantaviruses in the United States occurred in 1993 in the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah [14,15]. Patients passed away from fever, myalgias, thrombocytopenia, and pulmonary edema with hypotensive shock, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the presence of SNV and its deer mouse reservoir. The spread of SNV was later associated with the 1991–1992 El Niño event, which caused warmer winters and increased spring rainfall, inciting a boom in the rodent population and promoting viral spread [14,15]. ANDV was first detected during a small outbreak in the Patagonia region of southern Argentina in 1995, with the first major outbreak of ANDV occurring in 2018–2019 in Epuyén, Argentina, where three distinct superspreader events occurred with no relation to inciting exposure to a rodent reservoir, confirming its ability to spread between humans [16]. A schematic showing all major hantavirus outbreaks to date. Descriptive boxes are color-coded according to the type of hantavirus (Old World or New World) responsible, with the exception of the MV Hondius outbreak, which is highlighted red for emphasis. Additionally, regions with endemic hantaviruses are colored according to whether the endemic strain is an Old World (pink) or New World (blue) hantavirus. Image created in BioRender. The global burden associated with hantaviruses reflects two divergent clinical phenotypes. Old World viruses exhibit a case fatality rate (CFR) under 1% in settings with available vaccines and supportive care, whereas New World viruses carry an estimated CFR of 30–60% [17,18]. In 2025, eight countries in the Americas reported 229 cases of hantaviral infections with a CFR of 25.7%. 1,885 cases were reported across Europe in 2023, and thousands of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) cases have been reported annually in East Asia [7]. Molecular virology and host-virus interactions Hantaviruses (class Bunyaviricetes, order Elliovirales, family Hantaviridae) [19–21] are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with a segmented genome (11–13 Kb) consisting of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments, and are associated with an envelope protein containing viral glycoproteins [22,23]. In 2024, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) accepted a proposal to rename the class Ellioviricetes to Bunyaviricetes in RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) phylogeny and to split the order Bunyavirales into two orders, a broader classification based on observations of increased clustering into the two distinct orders Elliovirales (including families Hantaviridae and Peribunyaviridae) and Hareavirales (including families Arenaviridae, Nairoviridae, and Phenuiviridae) [20,21,24]. Hantaviruses can be dichotomized into two classes based on their geographic distribution: Old World viruses and New World viruses (Fig 1). The key distinction between these classes is the symptoms they cause: Old World viruses cause HFRS, and New World viruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS or HCPS) [17,25]. ANDV exhibits broad tropism, infecting multiple human cell types, including those of the heart, brain, and lungs, particularly lung epithelial cells. It also induces cellular injury and inflammatory responses while suppressing lipid metabolic pathways in lung epithelial cells [26]. Though less common than pulmonary or cardiac manifestations, New World hantaviruses, particularly ANDV, have also been shown to induce neurological manifestations, such as confusion, meningoencephalitis, pituitary apoplexy, and, albeit rarely, seizures, myelitis, and peripheral neuropathy [27]. Gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, have also been observed in ANDV-infected patients, both preceding and in tandem with the onset of cardiovascular symptoms [28]. However, more investigation is needed to better understand the frequency of onset, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and the clinical significance of these symptoms. Since the 1950s [29,30], hantaviruses have been identified on every inhabited continent, with pathogenicity varying substantially across strains [22,23]. The differences in pathogenic mechanisms and disease outcomes among viral strains can be partly determined by viral-encoded factors, with several viral entry mechanisms elucidated in recent years. The viral M genome segment encodes glycoprotein precursors that are processed into Gn and Gc subunits, which form tetrameric complexes that help mediate cellular entry [31]. New World hantaviruses utilize protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to directly engage viral Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes and facilitate entry into vascular endothelial cells [32,33]. Recent investigations have elucidated the higher-order lattice architecture formed by Gn/Gc heterotetramers on the hantaviral surface, highlighting their role as the primarily necessary and sufficient proteins for viral attachment and entry [34,35]. Analysis of these surface spikes indicates that Gn/Gc complexes may serve as potential targets for antiviral immunotherapeutic interventions, including neutralizing antibodies and structure-guided immunogens [36]. Upon viral entry and genome uncoating in the host-cell cytoplasm, the negative-strand genomes are transcribed into positive-strand mRNA by the viral RdRp. Similar to some other negative-sense RNA viruses, the hantaviral RdRp can also snatch 5’-capped mRNA fragments from host-cell transcripts, allowing the virus to use these sequences as primers for transcription and replication of the viral genome [37]. The nucleocapsid protein engages the viral RdRp and host ribosomes to selectively enhance translation of viral transcripts, while also interfering with protein kinase R (PKR) dimerization and remodeling of host proteostasis pathways, blunting cell-intrinsic antiviral defenses and promoting overall immune evasion [38,39]. Additionally, pathogenic hantaviruses have been shown to dampen early type I interferon (IFN) signaling in infected endothelial cells, thus sensitizing these cells to VEGF-mediated permeability [40,41]. This mechanism may underlie the pathogenesis of HFRS and HCPS. Hantaviruses can evade immune mechanisms by using structural and nonstructural proteins, such as NSs, NP, and Gn, to block RIG-I/MDA5-TBK1 signaling, antagonize IFN induction, and induce TUFM/LC3B-mediated mitophagy to degrade MAVS, respectively [42]. Of particular concern is the capacity of these viruses to evolve, driven by the error-prone RdRP, genetic reassortment events in the L segment, and hypervariable regions in the nucleocapsid protein encoded by the S segment [43,44]. Additionally, the lack of immunity in humans increases the capacity for viral transmission and virulence. This is especially concerning given recent epidemiological trends in Argentina, which suggest that ANDV has a CFR of 34%, even higher than that of strains detected between 2019 and 2025 [45]. Phylogenetic analysis of the ANDV M-segment coding region against reference strains from NCBI revealed that the novel strain associated with the MV Hondius outbreak [46] shares 94.26% sequence identity with the ANDV reference sequence (NC_003467.2), indicating evolutionary divergence from the reference strain (Fig 2). Further comparison of this novel M-segment sequence against the NCBI Core Nucleotide Database identified closely related ANDV sequences isolated from human whole blood samples collected in Argentina (south variant) in 2018 (MN258191 and MN258192). These findings suggest that the lineage most closely related to this novel strain may have been circulating in human populations and/or reservoir hosts for nearly eight years, while gradually accumulating mutations over time. Consistent with this inference, the novel strain’s M-coding region shows the highest sequence identity with the 2018 isolates (99.0% and 98.98%, respectively). Notably, the presence of 35 nucleotide mutations but only three amino acid substitutions, two in G1 (T193A and T516I) and one in G2 (A994T), within the glycoprotein-coding regions suggests strong purifying (negative) selection, preserving critical Gn and Gc functions. Overall, these findings indicate that the functional and transmission-relevant properties of ANDV are conserved across strains despite the accumulation of silent (synonymous) mutations, underscoring the importance of sustained genomic surveillance [47]. Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree constructed using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates (purple circles) for 38 M-segment sequences from the genus Orthohantavirus, including 35 species from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) RefSeq database, 2 species from GenBank (italicized), and 1 ANDV sequence (red font) obtained from a Swiss resident who had traveled on the MV Hondius cruise ship [46]. The clade containing the ANDV strain responsible for the current 2026 outbreak is highlighted in the pink box. Sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7.526, and the resulting alignment was used for ML phylogenetic tree construction in IQ-TREE. Human-to-human transmission of ANDV ANDV is unique in its capacity for human-to-human transmission, first suspected during the 1996 El Bolsón and Bariloche, Argentina, outbreaks and later confirmed at the molecular level soon after [48,49]. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak subsequently provided the most extensive documentation of this transmission route, as it was notable for three distinct superspreader events without any identifiable rodent exposure [50]. Although few additional ANDV outbreaks have been recorded, the MV Hondius outbreak provided further epidemiologic observations supporting this transmission route, including secondary cases among close contacts of symptomatic passengers [51]. It should be noted that, given the limited availability of outbreak-associated sequences and lack of continuous temporal sampling, we have avoided inferring direct or continuous viral transmission. Further investigation is needed to better establish the precise mechanisms, viral tropism for upper and lower respiratory tract airway epithelium, infectiousness duration, and full spectrum of transmission routes. Clinical management and therapeutics Management of hantaviral infections primarily consists of supportive care, with early detection and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in the cardiopulmonary phase remaining the most consistent determinants of survival [52,53]. Although Hantavax, an inactivated bivalent vaccine against HTNV, and a vaccine against SEOV are in active use across China and South Korea, no FDA-approved antivirals or vaccines are currently available for use in Western populations [53]. Several antiviral candidates have been investigated. Vandetanib demonstrated semi-prophylactic efficacy in Syrian hamsters [54], while ribavirin, though promising in animal models, has generally not shown robust efficacy in human clinical trials [55–58]. Additionally, polymerase-targeted antiviral strategies have been investigated in other members of Bunyaviricites, with molnupiravir showing inhibitory activity against RdRp of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (order Hareavirales, family Nairoviridae) [59]. However, further extensive studies are required to develop and evaluate direct-acting antiviral approaches in hantaviruses. Our team has previously identified potential antiviral candidates, including favipiravir and urolithin B, that demonstrate potent in vitro activity against ANDV [26]. Favipiravir, both when used alone and in combination with ribavirin, has been shown to exhibit antiviral activity against Old World HTNV [60]. These compounds were shown to restore cellular metabolism in infected cells, thus warranting further preclinical evaluation and clinical trials. To date, most assessed antiviral candidates have only shown promise in vitro or in animal models. It should be noted, however, that one patient from the MV Hondius was treated with a combination of intravenous and oral ribavirin, favipiravir, icatibant, and baricitinib, showing complete clinical resolution of viral symptoms after 10 days [61], which highlights the potential importance of combination therapies comprising direct-acting antivirals (e.g., favipiravir) and host-targeted treatments (e.g., icatibant and baricitinib) during late stages of disease. Lessons learned and a call to action The current outbreak has highlighted the need for improved infection prevention, detection, and surveillance infrastructure worldwide. Our current public health infrastructure can be better optimized to respond rapidly to outbreaks of neglected zoonotic pathogens, such as hantaviruses. As ANDV can spread through contact with infected rodents or their urine, saliva, or feces, surveillance and early ecological warning must be prioritized, including regular monitoring of rodent reservoir populations in high-incidence areas. It has been demonstrated that a synchronous, rapid increase in rodent populations in northwestern Argentina predictably preceded an HPS outbreak in 2023 [16,62]. As climate change continues to alter the geographic range and abundance of vector-borne organisms, the risk posed to global populations by hantaviruses could expand su…

full_text_sections.full_text: Figures Abstract In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infrastructure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical management, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases. A primer on the MV Hondius outbreak Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus capable of human-to-human transmission, underscoring its potential for outbreaks that extend beyond the traditional rodent-to-human route. This significance became particularly clear in May 2026, when the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of several cases of severe respiratory illness aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship carrying 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries, as it transited the South Atlantic from Argentina. Only a few days later, at least 13 cases, including three deaths, were identified and/or laboratory-confirmed, including secondary cases among contacts of the index patient [1], as well as plane passengers in close proximity to confirmed cases on a flight to South Africa [2] and a repatriation flight from Tenerife [1–6]. Contact tracing and quarantine measures were coordinated through the WHO National IHR (International Health Regulations) Focal Points and implemented across several countries, including the United Kingdom, South Africa, and the United States [2,3,7–10]. However, this outbreak is not the only recent notable case of hantaviral spread. In 2025, Betsy Arakawa, the wife of renowned actor Gene Hackman, passed away due to hantavirus infection in New Mexico, as did three people in Mammoth Lakes, California [11,12]. Hantavirus outbreaks highlight the challenge posed to public health agencies by neglected zoonotic pathogens—especially those that are ecologically complex, geographically distributed, understudied, and underfunded, yet capable of causing lethal outbreaks with little to no warning, thereby creating major public health concerns. As such, we aim to synthesize a brief primer on our current knowledge of hantaviruses and to propose areas for further research and development of emergency preparedness and capacity building within existing public health infrastructure. papers.title: Molecular surveillance of Bartonella species, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses in wild small mammals and their associated chigger mites in South Korea.
papers.abstract: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Molecular surveillance incorporating both small mammals and their associated ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife-ectoparasite interface. In this study, 1,444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites, analyzed as 680 host-associated pools, were collected from 17 sites in South Korea between 2022 and 2025. Samples were examined for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR- and RT-PCR-based methods, followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses. The predominant small-mammal species, Apodemus agrarius, accounted for 84.9% of captured small mammals. DNA related to Bartonella schoenbuchensis was detected in 473 of 680 chigger mite pools (69.6%), whereas DNA related to Bartonella bacilliformis, Bartonella henselae, and Bartonella taylorii was detected in three of 1,444 small-mammal liver samples (0.2%) for each taxon. DNA of Coxiella burnetii was detected in 51 of 1,444 liver samples (3.5%), all collected during the autumn 2024 survey. Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 37 small mammals (2.6%), predominantly in A. agrarius (35/37, 94.6%), with the remaining two detections in Crocidura spp. (2/37, 5.4%), and in three chigger mite pools (0.4%). To our knowledge, these findings provide the first molecular evidence of DNA related to B. schoenbuchensis in host-associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA related to B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small-mammal liver samples in South Korea. The results provide descriptive baseline data for wildlife-based molecular surveillance; they do not establish seasonal patterns, individual-mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

analysis.background: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens, underscoring the need for surveillance.
analysis.methods: From 2022–2025, 1,444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites (pooled into 680 host‑associated samples) were collected at 17 sites in South Korea; liver tissues and mite pools were screened for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR/RT‑PCR followed by sequencing and phylogenetic analysis.
analysis.results: Apodemus agrarius comprised 84.9% of captures. Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA was detected in 69.6% of chigger pools, while Bartonella bacilliformis, B. henselae, and B. taylorii each appeared in 0.2% of mammal livers. Coxiella burnetii DNA was found in 3.5% of livers, all during autumn 2024. Orthohantavirus RNA occurred in 2.6% of mammals, predominantly A. agrarius (94.6%) and also in Crocidura spp. (5.4%), and in 0.4% of chigger pools.
analysis.contribution: The study provides the first molecular evidence of B. schoenbuchensis in host‑associated chigger mites and the first reports of B. bacilliformis and B. henselae DNA in wild small‑mammal livers in South Korea, establishing baseline data for wildlife‑based molecular surveillance.
analysis.limitations: The findings are descriptive and do not establish seasonal patterns, individual‑mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens, underscoring surveillance needs. Methods: From 2022–2025, 1,444 mammals and 12,869 chigger mites (680 pools) from 17 South Korean sites were PCR/RT‑PCR screened for Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses with sequencing. Results: Apodemus agrarius made up 84.9% of captures; B. schoenbuchensis DNA was in 69.6% of mite pools, other Bartonella spp. in 0.2% of livers; C. burnetii in 3.5% of livers (autumn 2024); orthohantavirus in 2.6% of mammals (94.6% A. agrarius) and 0.4% of mite pools. Contribution: First molecular evidence of B. schoenbuchensis in chiggers and of B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in Korean wild mammals, providing baseline surveillance data. Limitations: Findings are descriptive and do not establish seasonal patterns, individual‑mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

papers.title_zh: 在韩国野生小型哺乳动物及其相关恙螨中对巴尔通体属、Coxiella burnetii和正汉坦病毒进行分子监测。

analysis_zh.background: 野生小型哺乳动物是多种人畜共患病原的关键宿主,凸显监测的必要性。
analysis_zh.methods: 2022–2025年,在韩国17个地点共采集1,444只野生小型哺乳动物及12,869只相关恙螨(合并为680个宿主相关样本),对肝组织和螨池进行PCR/RT‐PCR筛查巴尔通体属、Coxiella burnetii和正汉坦病毒,随后进行测序和系统发育分析。
analysis_zh.results: Apodemus agrarius占捕获总数的84.9%。在恙螨池中检测到Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA,检出率为69.6%;而Bartonella bacilliformis、B. henselae和B. taylorii分别出现在0.2%的哺乳动物肝脏中。Coxiella burnetii DNA在3.5%的肝脏中检出,全部发生于2024年秋季。正汉坦病毒 RNA在2.6%的哺乳动物中出现,主要为A. agrarius(94.6%),亦见于Crocidura属(5.4%),并在0.4%的恙螨池中检出。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究首次在宿主相关恙螨中提供B. schoenbuchensis的分子证据,并首次报告B. bacilliformis和B. henselae DNA出现在韩国野生小型哺乳动物肝脏中,为基于野生动物的分子监测奠定基线数据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本研究为描述性结果,未能确定季节性模式、单个螨的感染率或媒介能力。

papers.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April-May 2026.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

papers.title_zh: 比较田鼠肾脏和呼吸上皮细胞对不同正汉坦病毒的转录组响应

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物携带的病毒,可通过气溶胶传播导致人类疾病;在自然宿主中感染通常无症状,但人类疾病伴随免疫反应过度;由于栖息地变化和病毒重配导致的疫情增多,引发公共卫生关注。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者对来自感染三种不同正汉坦病毒的田鼠肾脏和呼吸上皮细胞进行比较性RNA测序和转录组分析。
analysis_zh.results: 转录组分析发现了共同以及病毒和组织特异的调控通路,突出显示了可能导致不同感染结果的复杂先天免疫和抗病毒信号响应。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物携带的病毒,可通过气溶胶传播导致人类疾病;在自然宿主中感染通常无症状,但人类疾病伴随免疫反应过度;由于栖息地变化和病毒重配… 方法：作者对来自感染三种不同正汉坦病毒的田鼠肾脏和呼吸上皮细胞进行比较性RNA测序和转录组分析。 结果：转录组分析发现了共同以及病毒和组织特异的调控通路,突出显示了可能导致不同感染结果的复杂先天免疫和抗病毒信号响应。 贡献：该研究深化了对自然宿主中宿主细胞相互作用和抗病毒通路的认识,为汉坦病毒的监测和潜在防控策略提供参考。 局限：提供的证据中未报告样本量、实验设计和定量结果的细节。

papers.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
papers.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

analysis.summary_en: Background: In 2026 a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak caused by Andes virus occurred on a cruise ship, raising concerns about viral spread in mobile populations. papers.title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Among the 28 vaccinees (11 farmers, 11 students, and 6 teachers), 9 were male and 19 were female, with a median age of 31 years. Sera from HFRS patient and vaccinees were all tested positive for HV IgG antibodies. Based on the typing criteria, of the 48 HFRS patient sera, 23 (47.92%) were identified as HTNV infection, 13 (27.08%) were SEOV infection, and the remaining 12 sera were untypable. Inter-individual variation in neutralizing capacity against HV vaccine and epidemic strains Among the 48 HFRS patient sera, 33 showed higher neutralizing titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26, with most differences within 2-fold. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. In contrast, neutralizing titers against the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were generally lower than those against the epidemic strain LN03. Nearly half of the sera showed ≥4-fold higher titers against LN03 than against L99. Furthermore, immunogenicity differed between the two SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17; 83.33% (40/48) of sera exhibited higher neutralizing titers against LN03 than against FJ-17. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). analysis_zh.methods: 使用一种含有汉滩病毒(HTNV)和首尔病毒(SEOV)株的双价灭活疫苗;筛选了康复期肾综合征出血热患者和接种者的血清,并通过ELISA法微中和试验测定针对疫苗株84FLi、L99以及流行株SX26、LN03、FJ-17的中和抗体滴度。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,汉坦病毒的遗传多样性和免疫原性呈地域差异;交叉中和抗体虽有差异但仍足够,说明当前疫苗能够提供广泛保护,但对不同株的效力可能存在差异,强调需持续监测并进行疫苗株匹配。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8+ regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8+ T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8+ Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

analysis.background: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus, virus‑specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology.
analysis.methods: The authors characterized an HLA‑E (Qa‑1)‑restricted CD8+ regulatory T‑cell subset in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model, including immunization with identified Qa‑1‑binding HTNV peptides and subsequent viral challenge.
analysis.results: CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+) were markedly reduced in patient peripheral blood and displayed a terminally differentiated, KLRG‑1‑high phenotype that correlated with disease severity; in mice, wild‑type animals immunized with the peptides showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas Qa‑1‑disrupted D227K mice cleared virus more efficiently but exhibited exacerbated renal pathology.
analysis.contribution: These findings indicate that HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, suggesting a trade‑off between pathology control and viral clearance and highlighting a potential therapeutic target.
analysis.limitations: The summary is based solely on abstract data; detailed methods, sample sizes, and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Hantaan virus, CD8+ T cells drive both clearance and immunopathology. Methods: Researchers characterized an HLA‑E‑restricted CD8+ regulatory T‑cell subset in patients and a murine HTNV model, using immunization with identified Qa‑1‑binding peptides followed by challenge. Results: CD8+ Tregs were reduced in patients and showed a terminal phenotype linked to severity; WT mice immunized with peptides had reduced renal pathology, while Qa‑1‑disrupted D227K mice cleared virus better but suffered worse renal damage. Contribution: The study shows HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Tregs limit immunopathology at the cost of delayed viral elimination, offering a therapeutic insight. Limitations: Only abstract information is available; detailed methodology and quantitative data are not reported.

papers.title_zh: CD8+ 调节性 T 细胞限制免疫病理,但削弱 汉滩病毒 感染中的病毒清除。

analysis_zh.background: 在由 汉滩病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)中,特异性病毒的 CD8+ T 细胞既介导病毒清除,也导致免疫病理。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者在肾综合征出血热患者和小鼠汉滩病毒感染模型中,对HLA‐E(Qa‐1)限制的CD8+调节性T细胞亚群进行表征,包括使用已鉴定的Qa‐1结合的汉滩病毒肽进行免疫接种,随后进行病毒挑战。
analysis_zh.results: 在患者外周血中,CD8+ Tregs(CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+)显著减少,表现出终末分化的KLRG‐1高表达表型,并与疾病严重程度相关;在小鼠中,免疫接种该肽的野生型动物肾脏免疫病理受抑制,而Qa‐1突变的D227K小鼠虽能更有效清除病毒,但出现加重的肾脏病理。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现表明,HLA‐E/Qa‐1限制的CD8+ Tregs能够在汉滩病毒感染期间抑制免疫病理,提示病理控制与病毒清除之间存在权衡,并突显其作为潜在治疗靶点的价值。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本摘要仅基于摘要数据,未报告详细方法、样本量和统计分析。

papers.abstract: Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event.
