Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Dispatch Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany Suggested citation for this article Abstract Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event. Despite being closely associated with human settlements for much of recent human history, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) were not domesticated as pets until the 17th and 18th Centuries in Japan (1). Wild brown rats, which are prolific synanthropic pests, harbor a great diversity of zoonotic agents (2,3). Pet rats, the domesticated form of brown rats, have likewise been associated with outbreaks of Leptospira spp. (4), Seoul virus (SEOV; Orthohantavirus seoulense) (5), and cowpox virus (6). SEOV is a zoonotic hantavirus found in both wild and pet rats globally (7). In Germany, pet rats have been linked to 4 detections of cases of human SEOV infection (5,8,9). Additional zoonotic pathogens in wild rats include the human pathogenic hepatitis E virus (HEV; Paslahepevirus balayani) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV; Rocahepevirus ratti). HEV is one of the main causative agents of acute hepatitis in humans worldwide and is typically transmitted through the fecal–oral route, consumption of undercooked pork, or blood and organ transplants. rHEV has been detected in wild brown rats and black rats (Rattus rattus) worldwide and is now recognized as a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis (10,11). Rats (Rattus spp.) are reservoirs of rHEV but have also been reported to be incidentally infected with genotype HEV-3 (12). To assess the presence of rHEV, HEV-3, and other related hepeviruses, as well as potential co-infection with SEOV and tissue distribution of hepevirus RNA and SEOV antigen in SEOV-infected and noninfected pet rats, we screened samples from 13 pet rats associated with 3 SEOV detections in human patients in Germany by molecular and serologic assays. Of those 13 pet rats, 11 tested positive for SEOV RNA in previous studies (5,9) (Appendix Table 1). We extracted RNA from liver tissue and screened it by a nested broad-spectrum reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) capable of detecting multiple HEV genotypes and rHEV (Appendix). By sequencing the RT-PCR products, we identified rHEV RNA in 3 of the 13 pet rats (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001), a finding further confirmed by rHEV-specific real-time RT-PCR (Appendix Table 1). The 3 pet rats, which were previously shown to be infected by SEOV (Appendix Table 1), came from 3 different owners; 2 rats were obtained from the same vendor and the source for the third rat was unknown (5,8,9). The 276 nt-long open reading frame (ORF) 1 and corresponding amino acid (aa) sequences of rHEV from the 3 pet rats were nearly identical (99.15%–100%) (Appendix Table 2). For further sequence comparisons and phylogenetic analyses, we downloaded 91 partial and 60 complete genome rHEV sequences from GenBank (Figure). In addition, we determined short ORF1 sequences of 12 wild brown rats from Rotterdam (n = 8) and Amsterdam (n = 4) (the Netherlands) that previously tested positive for rHEV RNA (2). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 3 pet rat–derived sequences were highly similar (98.55%–98.91%) to a wild rat–derived rHEV sequence from Rotterdam (M226) (Figure, panel A). A multiplex serology approach using bead-based Luminex technology (R&D Systems, https://www.rndsystems.com) (Appendix) detected rHEV-reactive antibodies in 12 of 13 pet rat blood samples; 3 of those 12 samples also showed reactivity to HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1). Subsequent Western blot analysis using the same 2 antigens mainly supported multiplex serology results: 11 of 12 multiplex serology–positive samples also tested positive for rHEV. Of the 11 seropositive samples, 10 also reacted in the Western blot assay with the HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1, Figure 1). That high seroprevalence suggests widespread circulation in pet rat breeding facilities, which should be confirmed using a larger sample size. In all 3 rHEV RNA–positive pet rats, rHEV-reactive antibodies were detected by multiplex serology. Differences in the results of multiplex serology and Western blot assay can be explained by differences in the epitope presentation and sensitivity of both assays. We obtained near-full rHEV genome sequences from the 3 pet rats from Germany (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001) and from 3 of the wild brown rats from the Netherlands by using a combination of high-throughput sequencing and RT-PCR–based sequence determination of the hypervariable genome region. The wild brown rats (M226, M268, and M186) from Rotterdam were selected for different levels of ORF1 sequence similarity to the 3 pet rat–derived sequences (Figure, panel A). The rHEV full genome sequences from the 3 pet rats were >99.7% identical, and nucleotide and amino acid sequences of all 4 ORFs and encoded proteins were >99.2% identical (Appendix Table 2). As in ORF1, the full genomes from the 3 German pet rats were most similar to the sequence from wild brown rat M226 from Rotterdam (full sequence >99.2% identical; each ORF >98.3%) (Appendix Table 3) and clustered with that sequence in the phylogeny (Figure, panel B). The most closely related rHEV sequences from Germany were detected in wild brown rats from Hamburg (Figure, panel B). The only sequence from a human patient in Germany (13) clustered among sequences from wild brown rats from Berlin, separate from the pet rat sequences (Figure, panel B; Appendix Table 3). On the basis of the complete coding sequences of pet rat–derived rHEV, we selected probe sequences to detect rHEV RNA through in situ hybridization in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues of the pet rats mounted on adhesive microscope slides (Appendix). We clearly detected a disseminated in situ hybridization signal using brightfield microscopy in the livers (hepatocytes) of rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001, confirming the rHEV quantitative RT-PCR results (Appendix Table 1, Figure 2). In addition, we detected an oligofocal in situ hybridization signal in the spleen of pet rat KS22/001 and in the intestinal lumen of pet rat KS19/1354. We detected no signal in the other tissues tested (Appendix Table 4). Nucleocapsid protein immunohistochemistry analysis of the rHEV-SEOV coinfected pet rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001 demonstrated SEOV antigen in multiple organs, predominantly the kidney and brain; antigen was detected less frequently in the spleen, intestine, liver, and lung (Appendix Tables 1, 3, Figure 2). That distribution is consistent with the previously described widespread endothelial tropism of SEOV in naturally infected wild rats and experimentally infected laboratory rats (14). In our study, advanced autolysis limited the assessment of pathological changes. We could not assess colocalization of both viruses because of insufficient tissue material. The co-infection of pet rats with the zoonotic pathogens SEOV and ratHEV and the rat-to-human transmission of SEOV in those cases (8,9) highlights a public health concern posed by pet rats. Unfortunately, the owners of the pet rats did not consent to providing blood samples; therefore, their rHEV serologic status could not be assessed. The near-identical rHEV sequences in the pet rats indicate a single incursion event consistent with potentially being independently obtained from the same vendor in Germany (5). The close similarity between the pet rat rHEV sequences and a wild rat–derived sequence from the Netherlands might indicate a wild rat origin of pet rat rHEV, further circulation by pet rat trade, and (at least mostly) uncoupled dynamics of rHEV in wild and captive rats. Owners and general practitioners should be aware of potential zoonotic risks associated with pet rats so that preventive hygienic measures can be taken and correct diagnosis supported. His research interests include the interplay between pathogen and host ecology, with a focus on small mammals. analysis.background: Pet rats are a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including hantaviruses and hepatitis E viruses.
analysis.methods: The study screened liver and blood samples from 13 pet rats in Germany that were linked to three human Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) infections (A19). RNA was extracted and tested with a nested broad‑spectrum RT‑PCR and a rHEV‑specific real‑time RT‑PCR (A21‑A22). Serologic status was assessed by bead‑based Luminex multiplex serology and confirmed by Western blot (A29).
analysis.results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats (23%) and the ORF1 sequences were 99.15‑100% identical (A25). The three sequences were 98.55‑98.91% similar to a wild‑rat rHEV strain from the Netherlands (A28). rHEV‑reactive antibodies were found in 12 of 13 rats, with 3 also reacting to HEV‑3 antigen (A29‑A30).
analysis.contribution: The findings show concurrent infection with SEOV and rHEV in pet rats and suggest a single incursion event, highlighting the need for surveillance of these zoonoses in pet‑rat breeding facilities (A3, A33).
analysis.limitations: The study examined only 13 rats, and the authors note that larger sample sizes are needed to confirm widespread circulation (A33); no formal limitation section is provided in the abstract.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pet rats are reservoirs of several zoonotic pathogens. Methods: Thirteen German pet rats linked to human SEOV cases were screened by RT‑PCR for rHEV and by Luminex/Western blot serology (A19‑A22, A29). Results: rHEV RNA was found in 3 rats (23%) with >99% sequence identity, and 12 rats had rHEV antibodies, three also reacting to HEV‑3 (A25‑A30). Contribution: The concurrent SEOV and rHEV infections and near‑identical sequences suggest a single incursion and underscore surveillance needs (A3, A33). Limitations: Small sample size and lack of a detailed limitations discussion (A33).

papers.title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by Hantaan virus is endemic across Eurasia and threatens renal failure and mortality; mechanisms are unclear due to lack of animal models. papers.title_zh: 一种针对 汉滩病毒 的NCG小鼠模型揭示了系统性感染和器官特异性细胞嗜性。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热由汉滩病毒引起,遍布欧亚大陆,构成严重的肾功能衰竭和死亡威胁。汉滩病毒感染机制尚不清楚,主要因缺乏易感动物模型。
analysis_zh.methods: 在高度免疫缺陷NCG小鼠中建立了系统性汉滩病毒感染模型;通过qRT-PCR定量病毒载量,并通过免疫荧光染色检视细胞亲和性与受体共定位。
analysis_zh.results: 汉滩病毒感染的NCG小鼠表现出强烈血症,并在肾脏、肺、脾脏、生殖器官和肝脏持续复制。病毒呈现组织特异性细胞亲和性,主要感染肾小管集合管间质细胞、肺泡上皮细胞和巨噬细胞,以及大脑和卵巢中的多种细胞群体。共定位分析提示肾细胞中潜在进入受体ITGB1和gC1qR,肺部AT1细胞和巨噬细胞中潜在进入受体ITGB1和ITGB2。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究结果表明NCG小鼠为研究汉滩病毒复制和系统性传播提供了有价值的体内模型。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;未报告详细方法、样本量、统计分析和定量数据。

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

MV 30 Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift 31 attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and 32 ecological opportunity. 33 Introduction 34 Andes hantavirus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and is 35 unusual among hantaviruses in its capacity for documented person-to-person 36 transmission1. ANDV has a tripartite negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome in 37 which the S segment encodes the nucleoprotein, the M segment encodes the 38 glycoprotein precursor that gives rise to Gn and Gc, and the L segment encodes the RNA- 39 dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)2. Historical sequencing is uneven across these 40 segments, with many isolates represented by only one or two segments and some M- 41 segment records available only as partial Gn/Gc sequences with separate accessions. 42 ANDV circulates primarily in the long-tailed colilargo (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), with 43 occasional detection in other rodents (e.g. Loxodontomys micropus, Abrothrix longipilis), 44 and repeatedly spill over into humans in Argentina and Chile3,4. The 2018-2019 Epuyén 45 outbreak5 and the 2026 MV Hondius-associated outbreak have therefore raised a central 46 question: are ANDV outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission driven by the 47 recent adaptive viral changes, or by the ecological emergence of pre-existing reservoir 48 lineages already capable of limited human transmission? Previous comparative work 49 proposed candidate mutations associated with person-to-person transmission6, but 50 whether independent outbreaks share a recurrent recent adaptive transition has not been 51 tested systematically. 52 These alternatives make different evolutionary predictions. Under a model of recent 53 adaptive emergence, independently arising human outbreaks should repeatedly be 54 preceded by one or more signatures of viral adaptation. These may include features such 55 as accelerated nonsynonymous evolution, signals of positive selection on outbreak- 56 lineage ancestral branches, convergent amino acid changes, or recurrent perturbation of 57 viral structures involved in entry, replication, immune evasion, or antigenicity. Under an 58 ecological-emergence model, outbreak lineages should instead be distributed across 59 standing reservoir diversity, retain strong geographic structure, and lack a reproducible 60 genomic transition immediately before their detection in humans. 61 For many emerging zoonoses, genomic epidemiology focuses on reconstructing 62 transmission chains after detection in humans. For reservoir-borne viruses, however, the 63 deeper question is often whether the human outbreak lineage can be placed within known 64 animal diversity and whether the branch leading to human emergence shows evidence 65 of accelerated or adaptive evolution. 66 This is particularly challenging for ANDV, for which available genomic data are sparse 67 and unevenly sampled across human and rodent hosts7. Available sequences include 68 known human outbreak clusters, rodent-associated genomes, and ANDV-like sequences 69 that have not always been consistently classified within major clades. Historical isolates 70 are also frequently represented by incomplete segment sets, resulting in substantial 71 differences in sequence availability across segments and sampling dates. These 72 characteristics can complicate molecular dating, as uneven temporal and host sampling 73 can distort the available temporal signal, while incomplete segment sampling and 74 uncertainty in clade classification can influence the inferred phylogenetic structure. 75 Together, these factors may affect evolutionary-rate and divergence-time estimates, and 76 potentially bias inferences about outbreak origins. 77 Here, we use the MV Hondius 2026 outbreak as an entry point into a broader comparative 78 analysis of ANDV evolution. We generated a paired blood- and nasal-derived S, M, and 79 L segment sequence from the outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked 80 collection of public human, rodent, and ANDV-like sequences, including incomplete and 81 partial genomes. We first reconstruct population-level diversity and introduce a linkage- 82 informed missing-segment framework for retaining sampled viruses in segment 83 alignments when a linked segment is unavailable. We then systematically infer molecular 84 rate estimates, evaluate the presence of time-dependent rate variation across nested 85 datasets and apply the Prisoner of War (PoW) model8 to examine deeper evolutionary 86 timelines of ANDV. Against this macroevolutionary background, we compare the 87 evolutionary emergence of MV Hondius outbreak with four earlier outbreaks involving 88 documented human-to-human transmission: i) a household and nosocomial transmission 89 chain in Southern Chile with five human infections in 2011 (Chile 2011)9 , ii) a three- 90 person transmission cluster in Argentina in 2014 (Argentina 2014)10 , iii) the largest known 91 ANDV outbreak with 34 confirmed infections in Argentina in 2018-2019 (Epuyén 92 2018/19)5, and iv) a two-person family cluster from Chile in 2024 (Chile 2024)11. We then 93 identify the closest sampled relatives and geographic context of each outbreak lineage, 94 reconstruct their evolutionary ancestry, and identify coding substitutions that arose along 95 the ancestral branch leading to each outbreak. By combining these reconstructions with 96 branch-rate, codon-selection, and structural analyses, we directly test whether repeated 97 human outbreaks share evidence of recent adaptive emergence while explicitly 98 accounting for the patchiness of the available genomic records. 99 Results 100 Phylogenetic placement and molecular dating of recorded ANDV human outbreaks 101 To best characterise the broader diversity that ANDV sits in, we first reconstructed 102 maximum-likelihood phylogenies for all publicly available S, M and L genome segments 103 of the Orthohantavirus andesense (Supplementary Figures 1-3). Consistent with 104 previous studies6, the five recorded human-to-human outbreak lineages fell within the 105 four main ANDV clades and were embedded within the broader rodent-associated ANDV 106 diversity. Our expanded curation additionally retains incomplete and partial genome 107 records, including rodent-derived isolates and the Chile 2011 human outbreak 4,9 that 108 would be lost by restricting analysis to complete three-segment genomes, thereby 109 broadening the reservoir context available for each outbreak. The closest sampled 110 relatives of the outbreak lineages were regionally structured. MV Hondius 2026 and Chile 111 2024 clustered within ANDV clade 3, together with rodent-derived (O. longicaudatus) 112 sequences4 and isolated human-infection sequences from Valdivia, Los Ríos, and San 113 Martín de los Andes, Neuquén, together with related Neuquén sequences9. This pattern 114 is consistent with a cross-border southern Chile-northern Patagonia assemblage rather 115 than a source confined to one national surveillance system (Figure 1A, Supplementary 116 Figures 1-3). The Argentina 2014 and Epuyén 2018/19 lineages were placed within 117 ANDV clade 2, whereas Chile 2011 fell within clade 1. No human-to-human transmission 118 has been documented yet for members of ANDV clade 4 (which contains the reference 119 ANDV genome, strain Chile-97178692), although it contains genomes derived from 120 isolated human infections. Several rodent-derived sequences fell within ANDV diversity 121 but outside clades 1-4. In particular, two well-supported groups were recovered in M and 122 S segments. Several other isolates also occupied positions outside clades 1-4, but these 123 placements were more weakly supported and/or inconsistent among genome segments. 124 These sequences may represent additional, previously under-recognised lineages of 125 ANDV. We refer to all of these sequences and clusters as “unclassified” (Supplementary 126 Figures 1-3). 127 The nearest sampled relatives of each outbreak lineage differed among genome 128 segments, owing to uneven sequence availability across the segmented genome (Figure 129 1). We refer to these non-outbreak human- or rodent-derived nearest relatives as 130 comparator sequences, because they provide the phylogenetic context for placing 131 outbreak lineages within broader ANDV diversity. The M segment contained the richest 132 set of nearby comparators for all outbreak lineages (total of 78 available ANDV M 133 segment sequences), followed by the S segment (70 available ANDV sequences). The L 134 segment had fewer nearby comparators and lacked equivalent closely related rodent- 135 derived sequences, limiting reservoir-inclusive inference (50 available ANDV sequences). 136 These differences in segment availability are central to the molecular dating problem 137 addressed below: although sequences from different segments may be linked to the same 138 isolate, observed-sequence-only alignments cannot represent that linkage when one or 139 more segments are missing. 140 Analysing only taxa with observed sequence data in each segment therefore produced 141 segment-specific datasets with different taxonomic compositions and, for a small subset 142 of clades, poorly resolved or unstable time trees. Rather than discarding incompletely 143 sequenced isolates, we developed a linkage-informed missing-segment representation 144 to retain known linkage without imputing sequence states (see Methods). If a sampled 145 virus had an observed sequence for at least one segment but lacked another, the missing 146 segment was represented by a genetically non-informative sequence (i.e., an all-N 147 sequence of the appropriate length) and assigned the same isolate identity and sampling 148 date. Its placement was constrained to the clade or internal relationship supported by the 149 linked observed segment(s), while unconstrained relationships remained estimated from 150 the segment-specific data. The approach therefore carries known linkage, sampling time, 151 and explicit cross-segment topology assumptions; it does not reconstruct the missing 152 sequence, and its assumptions can be violated by reassortment or uncertainty in the 153 constrained topology. We accordingly interpret linkage-informed estimates alongside the 154 observed-sequence dataset. 155 Observed-sequence S, M, and L trees placed outbreak-associated lineages and their 156 nearest comparators in broadly congruent positions (Figure 1A). Because missing- 157 segment taxa are constrained by linked segments, we assessed reassortment only in 158 observed-sequence trees. We found no well-supported segment discordance involving 159 the five outbreak lineages or their closest comparators, with the caveat that only M- 160 segment data are available for Chile 2011. Few placements differed among segments, 161 but most involved weakly supported nodes (posterior probability <0.8). Thus, 162 reassortment may have partly contributed to ANDV evolution, but it does not affect the 163 placement of the recent outbreak lineages analysed here. 164 Molecular clock behaviour and deeper evolutionary history of ANDV 165 We next systematically evaluated temporal signal and time-dependent rate variation 166 across nested ANDV datasets. For each genome segment, we analysed progressively 167 broader phylogenetic subsets comprising clade 2 alone; a combined clade 1 + clade 3 168 dataset containing only clades 1 and 3; clades 1-3 containing clades 1, 2 and 3; and 169 clades 1-4 containing all four major ANDV clades. Bayesian Evaluation of Temporal 170 Signal (BETS)12 compared heterochronous models incorporating the observed sampling 171 dates with otherwise equivalent isochronous models in which all tips were assigned the 172 same date (Methods). BETS supported the presence of temporal signal for all M- 173 segment datasets, and most S-segment datasets (except the clade1 + clade 3 datasets). 174 Temporal signal was weaker for the L-segment, consistent with fewer sequences, lacking 175 signal for clade 2, clade 1 + clade 3, and clade 1-3 datasets (Supplementary Table 4). 176 However, the inclusion of linkage-informed missing-segment taxa and the associated 177 constraints on the tree topology stabilised the time-scaled phylogeny, produced a 178 consistent rate estimate across independent runs, and restored support for temporal 179 signal by BETS (see Supplementary Table 4). This improvement was 182 particularly important for the more sparsely sampled L segment, where incomplete taxon 183 representation otherwise limited time-tree inference. 184 185 Figure 1. Time-scaled ancestry of the five documented ANDV human outbreaks across 186 genome segments. (A) Dated maximum clade credibility trees for the L, S, and M coding 187 sequences. Sequences of the MV 189 Hondius 2026 outbreak reported in this study are highlighted in pink and followed by an asterisk. 190 Nodes with posterior support below 0.8 are annotated with pink dots and their posterior support 191 value is shown next to them. (B) Posterior distributions for the closest sampled common ancestor 192 of each outbreak lineage under three sampling configurations: observed-sequence-only datasets 193 (“Observed”), observed-sequence datasets retaining two representatives per outbreak (“2pO”), 194 and linkage-informed datasets containing missing-segment taxa (“Linkage-informed”; labelled 195 “All” in the panel). Horizontal lines show posterior medians and box limits show 95% highest 196 posterior density intervals. 197 198 Across the nested datasets, posterior evolutionary rate estimates declined as older and 199 more divergent ANDV diversity was incorporated (Figure 2A, Supplementary Table 5). 200 Clade 2 tended to produce the highest rate estimates, whereas broader clade 201 combinations produced lower estimates. This systematic decline in inferred rate with 202 increasing phylogenetic depth is consistent with time-dependent rate variation. Across 203 different sampling configurations, rate estimates were comparatively stable except where 204 topology uncertainty was substantial, as in L clades 1+3. By contrast, closest-sampled- 205 ancestor dates were more sensitive to comparator representation (Figure 1B). The 206 principal value of the linkage-informed analysis is therefore not added sequence evidence 207 or guaranteed precision, but explicit representation and testing of known cross-segment 208 linkage and topology assumptions under patchy segment coverage. 209 Time-dependent rate variation is well described in RNA viruses, with short-term 210 evolutionary-rate estimates often exceeding those inferred over deeper timescales13. In 211 RNA viruses, this can arise because recent datasets retain transient polymorphisms and 212 mildly deleterious mutations that are later removed by purifying selection8. This 213 interpretation is also consistent with our codon-based analyses, which indicate that 214 purifying selection dominates most coding regions of the ANDV genome. In ANDV, the 215 effect may be particularly apparent because older pre-outbreak human- and rodent- 216 derived sequences can remain genetically very similar to much more recent outbreak 217 lineages. papers.title_zh: 近期人类暴发相关的安第斯病毒谱系的分子进化

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)独特地实现人际传播,提出了疫情是源于近期病毒适应还是源于已有的宿主储备系谱的疑问。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究从2026年MV Hondius暴发中获取血液和鼻腔来源的S、M、L片段基因组,并与人类、啮齿动物及ANDV样序列的片段关联集合合并;基于连锁信息的缺失片段框架在保持分离株身份和采样时间的同时,允许对片段覆盖不完整的敏感性分析;随后进行系统发育定年、时间依赖速率分析、选择检验、分支速率比较及结构映射。
analysis_zh.results: 在五次人类暴发中,系统发育定年将每个暴发系谱独立定位于地理结构化的宿主储备多样性中,最近的采样祖先早于检测出现;时间依赖速率分析显示更深的宿主储备相关历史,突变重建、选择检验、分支速率比较及结构映射均未发现在人传前的重复适应性转变;MV Hondius样本的共识水平分化极少。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现将关注点从反复的近期适应转向更深层的系谱特性和生态机会,为ANDV的监测和认识提供参考。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

analysis.background: Hantavirus spillover poses a growing public‑health threat, prompting a scoping review of mathematical models that address environmental drivers, One Health integration, and surveillance‑readiness gaps (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review maps modeling efforts across eco‑epidemiological pathways, evaluates One Health frameworks, and identifies surveillance preparedness deficiencies (A9).
analysis.current_state: Existing studies are catalogued in a curated metadata workbook and analytical scripts, showing a diverse but fragmented modeling landscape (A2).
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include limited integration of environmental and host data, insufficient One Health coordination, and inadequate surveillance‑readiness metrics (A9).
analysis.future_research: Future work should develop unified, reproducible models that embed environmental drivers, strengthen One Health collaboration, and generate actionable surveillance indicators (A9).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus spillover is a rising health concern, leading to a scoping review of mathematical models on environmental drivers, One Health, and surveillance gaps (A1). Main directions: The review surveys eco‑epidemiological modeling, One Health integration, and surveillance preparedness (A9). Current state: A curated metadata set and reproducible scripts reveal a varied but fragmented modeling corpus (A2). Gaps: Integration of environmental and host data, One Health coordination, and surveillance‑readiness metrics remain weak (A9). Future research: Build unified, reproducible models that incorporate environmental drivers, enhance One Health links, and produce actionable surveillance outputs (A9).

papers.title: Progress in antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus: Current advances and future perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-associated zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), two clinically distinct diseases characterized by vascular dysfunction and potentially severe organ failure. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, and recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. This review highlights the experimental and clinical evidence needed to advance promising antiviral and vaccine candidates toward effective strategies for prevention and treatment of hantavirus infections.

Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 2 of 23 Narrative Review Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, tripartite, negative-sense RNA viruses within the family Hantaviridae. The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. Recent surveillance data illustrate the continuing, geographically heterogeneous disease burden. In China, national surveillance recorded 3,271 cases of epidemic hemorrhagic fever and 16 deaths in 2025 [17]. In the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA), 1,885 hantavirus infections were reported in 2023, corresponding to a notification rate of 0.4 cases per 100,000 population [18]. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 229 confirmed cases of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and 59 deaths through epidemiological week 47 of 2025, corresponding to a reported case-fatality proportion of 25.7% [19]. These figures originate from different years, surveillance systems, and case definitions and should not be interpreted as directly comparable estimates of regional incidence or disease lethality. Despite this burden, supportive management remains the cornerstone of clinical care, and no antiviral has demonstrated consistent efficacy across HFRS and HCPS [9]. A randomized clinical trial conducted in China reported reduced mortality and selected complications among patients with HFRS receiving intravenous ribavirin [20]. However, a placebo-controlled trial in HCPS did not establish a clinical benefit during the cardiopulmonary phase, underscoring why treatment findings cannot be generalized across syndromes or disease stages [21]. Favipiravir has shown antiviral activity and improved survival under selected preclinical conditions [22]. RNA interference has suppressed Andes virus replication in cultured cells [23]. Neutralizing monoclonal antibodies have conferred protection in selected animal challenge models, but their efficacy in patients remains unconfirmed [24]. Collectively, these findings illustrate the different levels of evidence supporting current antiviral candidates, ranging from clinical investigation to in vitro and animal-model studies [25]. Prevention faces similar translational challenges. Inactivated vaccines targeting HFRS- associated hantaviruses have been implemented in China [26], while Hantavax is an authorized Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 3 of 23 Narrative Review inactivated Hantaan virus vaccine in South Korea [27]. In contrast, a bivalent Hantaan/Puumala DNA vaccine has reached phase IIa clinical evaluation for safety and immunogenicity, without demonstrating clinical effectiveness against naturally acquired infection [28]. Recombinant protein, viral vector-based, and messenger RNA vaccine platforms have been investigated predominantly in preclinical studies, and the breadth and durability of vaccine-induced protection remain important evidence gaps [29]. Accordingly, the aim of this narrative review is to critically evaluate the molecular rationale, evidence levels, and translational limitations of current hantavirus antiviral and vaccine strategies. The discussion first summarizes mechanisms relevant to therapeutic targeting and antigen design, then compares clinically investigated interventions with preclinical and exploratory approaches, assesses the development status of vaccine platforms, and identifies priorities for further experimental and clinical validation. Virology and pathogenesis of hantavirus Genome organization and viral structure The hantavirus genome comprises three RNA segments, each encoding proteins with distinct roles in the viral life cycle. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA and participates in viral RNA synthesis [1]. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which mediate viral attachment and membrane fusion [30]. Because Gn and Gc contain neutralizing antibody epitopes, they represent important targets for antibody-based interventions and vaccine antigen design [31−33]. Furthermore, the ability of Gn and Gc to self-assemble into virus-like particles in experimental expression systems provides a potential platform for vaccine antigen presentation [34]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is responsible for viral messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication [1]. During transcription, the viral transcription machinery uses short capped RNA primers acquired from host transcripts through cap-snatching to synthesize mRNA from negative-sense genomic RNA (vRNA) [35]. In contrast, genome replication proceeds through primer-independent synthesis of a full-length positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA), or antigenome, from the vRNA template [36]. The antigenome subsequently serves as an intermediate template for producing new negative-sense genomic RNA, rather than functioning as a protein-coding transcript [37]. These mechanistically distinct steps identify RdRp and viral RNA synthesis as relevant targets for direct-acting antivirals. In addition, experimental evidence demonstrating interactions between N and RdRp highlights the importance of the viral replication complex in RNA synthesis [38]. Viral entry and host interaction Hantavirus entry begins with Gn/Gc-mediated interactions with host-cell entry factors, followed by endocytosis and membrane fusion within endosomal compartments [13,30]. Earlier cell-based studies implicated αvβ3 integrins in entry by certain HFRS-associated hantaviruses [39]. In contrast, protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been experimentally identified as a critical entry factor for Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus in pulmonary endothelial cells. Disruption of PCDH1 expression also conferred protection against Andes virus challenge in hamsters [40]. These findings indicate that entry-factor dependence differs among hantaviruses and should not be represented as a single universal receptor pathway. For Hantaan virus, clathrin-dependent receptor-mediated endocytosis was demonstrated in a cell-based investigation, although this pathway should not be assumed to operate identically in all hantaviruses [41]. Gn and Gc contribute complementary functions to viral attachment, membrane fusion, and virion assembly [42]. Following entry, pathogenic hantaviruses primarily target vascular endothelial cells, where infection can impair barrier function without extensive direct viral cytolysis [13]. Experimental studies have linked enhanced vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling to increased endothelial permeability [14]. Specifically, Andes virus infection of human lung endothelial cells has been associated with increased VEGF production and reduced junctional VE-cadherin, Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 4 of 23 Narrative Review contributing to endothelial barrier disruption [43]. The resulting vascular leakage contributes to renal involvement in HFRS and pulmonary and cardiovascular complications in HCPS [4, 5, 44]. Furthermore, pathogenic hantaviruses have been shown to promote platelet adherence to infected endothelial cells in experimental systems, suggesting an additional mechanism contributing to vascular dysfunction [45]. Immunopathogenesis Host immune responses contribute to both control of hantavirus infection and the development of vascular injury. Innate recognition involving retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors activates type I interferon signaling and restricts Hantaan virus replication in experimental systems [46]. However, hantaviruses can modulate these antiviral pathways, and the outcome reflects interactions between viral replication and host immune regulation [37]. In a Hantaan virus model, viral interference with TRIM25-associated RIG-I-like receptor signaling was reported as a mechanism of innate immune antagonism [47]. Clinical observations in patients with Puumala virus infection further demonstrate the involvement of both innate and adaptive immune responses during hantavirus infection [48]. In addition, neutralizing antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoproteins can inhibit viral entry and represent important components of vaccine development and passive immunotherapy, although their protective breadth varies depending on the antibody and viral species [24,31]. Adaptive immune responses, particularly virus-specific T-cell responses, may contribute to viral control but can also participate in immunopathology. In an endothelial-cell culture model, hantavirus-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes increased permeability of infected endothelial monolayers, suggesting a potential mechanism of immune-mediated endothelial injury [49]. However, the extent to which this experimental mechanism contributes to vascular pathology in patients remains incompletely established. Dysregulated inflammatory mediators and VEGF- associated signaling may further impair endothelial junctions and amplify vascular leakage [14,15, 50]. These findings highlight the need to distinguish protective antiviral immunity from potentially harmful immune-mediated responses and support the investigation of Khairullah et al. Current antiviral strategies against hantavirus Current management of hantavirus infection relies primarily on supportive and organ-directed care, including respiratory and hemodynamic support and renal replacement therapy when clinically indicated [9]. Although several antiviral candidates have been investigated, their levels of supporting evidence and clinical development vary substantially. Ribavirin has undergone human clinical testing, with different outcomes reported between HFRS and HCPS [20,21]. In contrast, favipiravir [22], RNA interference-based approaches [23], and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies [24] remain supported predominantly by preclinical evidence from cell-based and animal studies. Additional compounds identified through cell-based screening have demonstrated potential to interfere with hantavirus entry, although their therapeutic relevance remains to be established [51]. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. papers.title: Persistent leukopenia masks hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) typically comes with fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and leukocytosis. However, atypical manifestations may obscure diagnosis. A 30-year-old man with rodent exposure had high fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia, without overt renal dysfunction despite mild renal involvement in the form of proteinuria. Hantaan virus was confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. The patient recovered following ribavirin and supportive management. This case highlights that in HFRS-endemic regions, hantavirus infection should be suspected among patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia rather than the typical leukocytosis, even without overt renal dysfunction.

papers.title: Assessing the performance of time series prediction models for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across different high-risk areas in Shaanxi Province, China
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a climate-sensitive disease. Existing forecasting models often overlook prefecture-level variations and environmental drivers. This study compares time series models incorporating environmental factors for prefecture-level HFRS prediction. Methods Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors were collected from 2005 to 2023 in four typical prefecture-level cities, including Xi'an, Baoji, Xianyang, and Weinan. Core factors were determined via stepwise screening. We developed four time series models: univariate seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) and long short-term memory (LSTM), alongside their multivariate counterparts with exogenous variables (SARIMAX and LSTMX). Specifically, multivariate models incorporated screened environmental drivers, whereas univariate models relied solely on historical epidemic data. Model robustness was further assessed by rolling-origin validation across three test years (2021−2023), in which the entire modeling pipeline was re-executed within each training window, and the sensitivity of LSTMX performance to the covariate-selection strategy was quantified. Results The predictive value of environmental covariates for HFRS forecasting varied by city and evaluation context. In Xi'an and Baoji, the multivariate LSTMX model showed lower forecasting errors (Xi'an: R 2 = 0.976, RMSE decreased from 69.246 to 17.782; Baoji: R 2 = 0.950, RMSE decreased from 6.694 to 2.805). Conversely, in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA yielded lower errors (R 2 = 0.940 and 0.889, respectively), and incorporating covariates did not reduce forecasting errors. Rolling-origin validation across 2021–2023 yielded a consistent ranking: LSTMX had the lowest mean RMSE in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models had lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the screened covariate set was the only strategy that never caused a severe loss of accuracy, whereas including all 14 environmental variables did not reduce errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Pairwise model differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction, and the city ranking changed when the models were refitted on the monthly crude incidence-rate scale; the rankings are therefore reported descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of regional differences in environmental effects. Conclusions No single forecasting configuration was uniformly optimal across cities: LSTMX with lagged environmental factors yielded the lowest errors in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models yielded lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan; however, these pairwise differences did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction and changed under the incidence-rate scale. When extending these models to new settings, both univariate and covariate-enhanced configurations should be compared.

papers.title_zh: 评估时间序列预测模型在中国陕西省不同高风险地区对肾综合征出血热的表现

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种气候敏感性疾病,现有预测模型常忽视地级市层面的差异和环境驱动因素。
analysis_zh.methods: 收集了2005‐2023年四个地级市(西安、宝鸡、咸阳、渭南)的月度肾综合征出血热病例数及14项环境因素;通过逐步筛选确定核心因素;构建了四种时间序列模型(SARIMA、LSTM、SARIMAX、LSTMX),其中多变量模型使用筛选后的环境驱动因子,并在2021‐2023年采用滚动起点验证进行评估。
analysis_zh.results: 在西安和宝鸡,使用多变量LSTMX得到最低误差(西安 R2=0.976,RMSE 从 69.246 降至 17.782;宝鸡 R2=0.950,RMSE 从 6.694 降至 2.805)。在咸阳和渭南,单变量SARIMA表现最佳(R2=0.940 和 0.889),加入协变量未降低误差。滚动起点验证确认了这些城市特异的排名;敏感性分析显示,筛选后的协变量保持了预测精度,而使用全部14个变量未能改善误差。经 Holm 校正后,两两模型差异未达统计显著性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,最佳肾综合征出血热预测配置因城市而异,建议在推广至新地区时比较单变量模型和加入协变量的模型。
analysis_zh.limitations: 两两模型差异未达统计显著性,且在以发病率尺度重新拟合模型后排名发生变化;结论仅基于摘要层面的证据。

papers.title: Hantavirus infection and the boundaries of autoimmunity: Vascular immunopathology, autoimmune-like mimicry, and post-infectious phenomena.
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses causing acute systemic vascular syndromes, principally haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although primarily infectious, hantavirus disease may generate vascular, renal, haematological, and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune-mediated disorders. This Review critically examines the boundary between infection-driven immunopathology and autoimmunity. Hantavirus infection involves endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine and chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis, and adaptive immune responses, whose expression is further influenced by virus-, host-, and tissue-specific factors. These mechanisms contribute to the marked heterogeneity of clinical disease and may reproduce autoimmune-like clinical and laboratory features, but do not, in themselves, establish sustained loss of immune tolerance. Current evidence is substantially stronger for acute infection-associated immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry than for persistent autoreactivity or causally attributable post-infectious autoimmune disease. Reported autoimmune phenomena remain uncommon and predominantly case-based, while longitudinal, antigen-specific, and epidemiological evidence is limited. Persistent or recurrent manifestations after resolution of infection therefore require additional serological, histopathological, or other objective evidence of sustained immune dysregulation. Hantavirus infection thus provides a clinically informative model for distinguishing antiviral immunopathology from autoimmune-like mimicry and rare possible post-infectious autoimmunity, with direct implications for diagnosis and therapeutic restraint. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses that cause acute systemic vascular syndromes such as haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review discusses how hantavirus disease can generate vascular, renal, haematological and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune‑mediated disorders, highlighting mechanisms like endothelial dysfunction, interferon responses, cytokine storms, complement activation and immunothrombosis (A2).
analysis.current_state: Evidence strongly supports acute infection‑driven immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry, whereas data for sustained autoreactivity or post‑infectious autoimmune disease are limited (A6).
analysis.gaps: Reported autoimmune phenomena are uncommon, largely case‑based, and lack longitudinal, antigen‑specific or epidemiological confirmation (A7).
analysis.future_research: Future work should obtain serological, histopathological and other objective markers of persistent immune dysregulation after hantavirus infection to clarify rare post‑infectious autoimmunity (A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses cause acute vascular syndromes (A1). Main directions: The review examines overlapping vascular, renal and systemic phenotypes with immune‑mediated disorders and underlying mechanisms such as endothelial dysfunction and cytokine amplification (A2). Current state: Acute infection‑driven immunopathology is well documented, while persistent autoimmunity evidence is weak (A6). Gaps: Autoimmune reports are rare, case‑based, and lack robust longitudinal data (A7). Future research: Obtain serological, histopathological and other objective evidence of sustained immune dysregulation post‑infection (A8).

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒感染与自身免疫边界:血管免疫病理、自身免疫样模仿及感染后现象。

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物携带的RNA病毒,可导致急性系统性血管综合征,如肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征(A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述讨论了汉坦病毒疾病如何产生血管、肾脏、血液学和系统性表型,这些表型与免疫介导的疾病重叠,强调了内皮功能障碍、干扰素应答、细胞因子风暴、补体活化和免疫血栓形成等机制(A2)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 证据强有力地支持急性感染驱动的免疫病理和表型模拟,而关于持续自身反应性或感染后自身免疫疾病的数据有限(A6)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 已报告的自身免疫现象罕见,主要基于个案,且缺乏纵向、抗原特异性或流行病学的确认(A7)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来的研究应获取汉坦病毒感染后持续免疫失调的血清学、组织病理学及其他客观标志,以阐明罕见的感染后自身免疫(A8)。

papers.title: A single-amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒导致 汉坦病毒肺综合征,且偶有涉及人际传播的罕见暴发。
analysis_zh.methods: 将一次暴发中分离的人类安第斯病毒株与同一区域的啮齿动物分离株在叙利亚金仓鼠中比较致死性。
analysis_zh.results: 基因组测序发现25个非同义置换,其中包括糖蛋白前体的T641I突变;两株在生长动力学上存在差异,人类株虽病毒RNA合成相似,但病毒释放延迟;在人类细胞表达实验中,I641T置换降低了高尔基体滞留并加速了类病毒颗粒的释放。
analysis_zh.contribution: T641I突变可能是人类适应性改变,能够改变糖蛋白转运并增强病毒外排,从而推动对安第斯病毒致病性和传播机制的认识。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细方法、样本量及统计分析。

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. CASE PRESENTATION: A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. CONCLUSION: Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

source_records.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
source_records.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

analysis.future_research: Standardized, multicenter validation studies are needed to develop robust early warning systems for precise management of severe HFRS.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS remains a major public health issue, requiring early identification of severe cases. Current state: Bedside signs and routine labs consistently predict severity, and immunological dysregulation offers mechanistic support. Gaps: Lack of external validation and clinical implementation hampers utility. Future research: Multicenter, standardized validation of early warning systems is essential.

papers.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. METHODS: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 分子诊断与病毒RNA动力学,使用仅限研究用途的RT-PCR检测:西班牙一家三级医院的经验。

analysis_zh.background: 本研究旨在评估一种商业化的RUO实时RT-PCR检测用于安第斯病毒检测在西班牙首次输入性暴发期间的临床性能和定性一致性。
analysis_zh.methods: 对14名因安第斯病毒(ANDV)暴发而遣返的人员进行全血和血清筛查;对其中2例确诊病例进行前瞻性监测,按每72小时采集一次全血、血清、口咽拭子、尿液和直肠拭子标本。标本在BSL-3设施中灭活,自动提取RNA,并使用RealStar® 汉坦病毒‐HPS RT‐PCR检测;所有标本亦在西班牙国家参考实验室采用汉坦病毒特异性RT‐PCR参考方法进行分析,评估定性一致性、Ct值相关性及病毒RNA动力学。
analysis_zh.contribution: RealStar® 汉坦病毒‐HPS RT‐PCR检测与参考方法表现出高度定性一致性,在暴发调查和纵向随访中提供了及时的分子信息;全血可能有助于安第斯病毒RNA的纵向检测,尽管结果为描述性,未能确立普遍的病毒脱落动力学或传染性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本研究结果为描述性,未能确立普遍的病毒脱落动力学或传染性;仍需进一步的分析和临床研究以确认该检测的性能和临床价值;目前仅有摘要信息可供参考。

papers.title: Hantavirus as a catalyst for urgent One Health preparedness in Africa: strengthening the human-animal-environment interface.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that exposes critical gaps in global and African health preparedness at the human-animal-environment interface. Although historically linked to outbreaks in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, recent events, including a 2026 multi-country Andes virus cluster associated with international travel, underscore its epidemic potential and rare human-to-human transmission. In Africa, no large-scale indigenous outbreaks have been confirmed; however, ecological suitability, weak surveillance systems, and limited diagnostic capacity suggest possible under-detection. This commentary examines global preparedness systems and contrasts them with structural and operational gaps in Africa, including weak laboratory capacity, fragmented surveillance, and limited One Health integration. It also highlights implementation challenges, such as resource constraints and workforce shortages. Beyond technical systems, behavioral and social factors - including risk perception, community engagement, and trust - are essential to effective outbreak response. Strengthening One Health preparedness through laboratory investment, workforce training, regional collaboration, and community-based risk communication is essential to improving resilience against emerging zoonotic diseases.
